Sagāthāvagga Samādhisutta (The Discourse on Concentration) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when concentration is developed and cultivated, it yields great fruit and brings great benefit. And how, bhikkhus, is concentration developed and cultivated so that it yields great fruit and brings great benefit? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops concentration with both the internal and external basis for the perception of light. He develops concentration with the basis for the perception of light both internally and externally. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that concentration is developed and cultivated so that it yields great fruit and brings great benefit. [The Buddha said: “Bhikkhus, there are these four bases for the perception of light. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells perceiving the visible forms of this world internally while seeing the visible forms of that world externally, and he is intent upon their beauty. This is the first base for the perception of light. Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells perceiving the visible forms of that world externally while seeing the visible forms of this world internally, and he is intent upon their beauty. This is the second base for the perception of light. Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having transcended the perception of visible forms internally, sees visible forms externally, and he is intent upon their beauty. This is the third base for the perception of light. Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having entirely surmounted the perception of visible forms, enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, and he is intent upon its beauty. This is the fourth base for the perception of light. These, bhikkhus, are the four bases for the perception of light. “Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings.
Which three?
Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”
"These, monks, are the three feelings.
Composed, clearly comprehending,
and mindful, the disciple of the Buddha—
He understands feeling,
and the origin of feelings,
and where they cease.
And the path leading to their destruction;
with the destruction of feelings,
the bhikkhu is free from hunger and has attained final nibbāna.”

Sagāthāvagga (The Chapter with Verses)
The Discourse on Happiness:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings.
Which three?
"Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
these, monks, are the three feelings.
Whether pleasant or painful...
Together with that which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant—
whatever is felt, whether internal or external.
Having known this as suffering—
subject to dissolution and destined for decay—
and seeing its passing away again and again,
"In this way, one becomes dispassionate toward it.

*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 36.3 (SN 36.3, PTS SN iv 205).
1. Sagāthāvagga Pahānasutta:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings.”
Which three?
Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Monks, the underlying tendency to lust must be abandoned regarding pleasant feeling; the underlying tendency to aversion must be abandoned regarding painful feeling; and the underlying tendency to ignorance must be abandoned regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
But when, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling,
the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling, and the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
then, monks, he is called a bhikkhu who is free from underlying tendencies, one of right vision, who has cut off craving, turned away [from the round], and attained the destruction of the taints.
‘Through the full realization of conceit, he has brought an end to suffering.
For one experiencing a pleasant feeling who does not understand that feeling;
Thus there is a latent tendency to lust for one who does not see the escape,
even while experiencing suffering.
For one who does not understand feeling,
and who does not see the escape from it, there exists the underlying tendency to aversion.
That peaceful state which is neither painful nor pleasant,
taught by the one of vast wisdom—
he who delights even in that, [is not free from craving].
One is not liberated from suffering.
But when a bhikkhu is ardent and does not neglect clear comprehension, [he is liberated].
Then that wise one fully understands all feelings; having fully understood feelings, he...
Taintless in this very life,
at the breaking up of the body, the knower of Dhamma who stands firm in Dhamma does not enter into reckoning.
The Third.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 36.4 (SN 36.4, PTS SN iv 206) 1.
Sagāthāvagga (The Chapter with Verses)
The Pātāla Sutta:
“Monks, when an uninstructed worldling speaks the words,
‘There is a bottomless abyss in the great ocean,’ [he speaks thus].”
But regarding this, monks, the uninstructed worldling speaks such a non-existent and unreal statement as:
“There is a Pātāla in the great ocean.
Monks, this term “Pātāla” is a designation for bodily painful feelings.
“Bhikkhus, when an uninstructed worldling is touched by a painful bodily feeling, he sorrows, languishes, and laments; he weeps beating his breast and falls into confusion.
This, bhikkhus, is called ‘the uninstructed worldling who has not risen up from the abyss and has not found a foothold.

“But, bhikkhus, when an instructed noble disciple is touched by a painful bodily feeling, he does not sorrow, does not languish, does not lament; he does not weep beating his breast and does not fall into confusion.”
“This, monks, is called a learned noble disciple who has risen from the abyss and found firm ground.
He does not tolerate these arisen painful feelings.”
Physical [pains] that take away life,
by which one who is touched trembles;
he cries out and weeps.
Weak and lacking in strength,
he did not rise up from the abyss,
nor did he find a firm footing.
But whoever endures these arisen painful feelings—
bodily, life-threatening— [is a true ascetic].
Touched by which one does not tremble—
he has indeed risen from the abyss and has moreover reached firm ground.
The Fourth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 36.5 (SN 36.5, PTS SN iv 207) 1.
Sagāthāvagga (The Chapter with Verses)
The Discourse on What Should Be Seen:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings.
Which three?
There are pleasant feelings, painful feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
Pleasant feelings, monks, are to be regarded as suffering; painful feelings are to be regarded as a dart; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are to be regarded as impermanent.
When, monks, a monk has seen pleasant feeling as suffering, painful feeling as a dart, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent—
“Monks, this one is called a bhikkhu who has seen rightly: he has cut off craving, stripped away the fetters, and by the complete penetration of conceit, he has made an end of suffering.
He who saw pleasure as suffering, and saw suffering as a dart;
That peaceful state which is neither painful nor pleasant,
he has seen as impermanent.
That bhikkhu is indeed one who sees rightly.
He fully understands feeling;
having fully understood feeling,
he is taintless in this very life.
"With the breakup of the body, the knower of the Veda, established in the Dhamma,
does not pass into reckoning.
Thus ends the fifth [sutta].

Sagāthāvagga Sallasutta – The Discourse on the Arrow “Bhikkhus, just as a man pierced by an arrow and smeared with poison might seek out a physician and surgeon, and that physician and surgeon would then extract that arrow from him with a sharp instrument; and while that arrow was being extracted, he would not think: ‘I am having this arrow extracted; it has been extracted; it will have been extracted. Rather, his concern would be only this: ‘How shall I be cured of this sickness? In the same way, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases of contact, he is called a noble disciple who has extracted the arrow, who has cut off craving, who has awakened to the Dhamma, and who has reached the end of suffering. What six? The eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base. When a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these six bases of contact, he is called a noble disciple who has extracted the arrow, who has cut off craving, who has awakened to the Dhamma, and who has reached the end of suffering.”
“Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling experiences a pleasant feeling, he experiences a painful feeling, and he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The instructed noble disciple also experiences a pleasant feeling, he experiences a painful feeling, and he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
In this regard, bhikkhus, what is the distinction, what is the specific intent, and what is the difference between the instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed worldling?”
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One...
Monks, when an uninstructed worldling, being touched by a painful feeling, sorrows, languishes, laments, beats his breast, weeps, and falls into confusion.
He experiences two kinds of feelings:”
It is both bodily and mental.
Just as if, monks, a man were pierced by an arrow,
and he were then pierced by a second arrow following the first.
"In this way, monks, that man experiences a sensation with two arrows.
In the same way, monks, when an uninstructed worldling is touched by a painful sensation, he sorrows, languishes, laments, beats his breast, weeps, and falls into confusion.
He experiences two sensations—"
It is both bodily and mental.
Furthermore, being touched by that same painful feeling, one becomes possessed of repulsion.
In one who is thus possessed of repulsion toward the painful feeling, the underlying tendency to repulsion toward painful feeling lies latent within.
Thus, being touched by painful feeling, he delights in sensual pleasure.
For what reason?
Because, monks, that uninstructed worldling does not understand the escape from painful feeling other than through sensual pleasure.
In one who delights in sensual pleasure, the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling lies latent.
Such a person does not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding those feelings.

In one who does not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding those feelings, the underlying tendency to ignorance toward neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling lies latent.
Thus, when one feels a pleasant feeling, one feels it while bound to it;
when one feels a painful feeling, one feels it while bound to it;
when one feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one feels it while bound to it.
“Monks, this is called ‘the uninstructed worldling who is bound by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is bound by suffering,’ I say.

But, monks, when the instructed noble disciple is touched by a painful feeling, he does not grieve, he does not waste away, he does not lament, he does not weep beating his breast, and he does not fall into confusion.
He experiences a single feeling:”
It is bodily, not mental.
Just as if, monks, a man were pierced by an arrow,
and he were not pierced through and through by a second arrow.
"In this way, monks, that man experiences a sensation with a single dart.

In the same way, monks, when a well-taught noble disciple is touched by a painful sensation, he does not grieve, does not languish, does not lament, does not beat his breast and weep, and does not fall into confusion.
He experiences a single sensation—"
It is bodily, not mental.
Furthermore, when touched by that same painful feeling, one does not harbor resentment.
Since one does not harbor resentment toward that painful feeling, the underlying tendency to resentment toward painful feeling does not lie latent within one.
Thus, being touched by a painful feeling, he does not delight in sensual pleasure.
Why is that? Because, monks, that learned noble disciple understands the escape from painful feeling other than through sensual pleasure.
For one who does not delight in sensual pleasure, the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling does not lie latent.
He understands, as it really is, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding those feelings.

For one who understands, as it really is, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding those feelings, the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling does not lie latent.
Thus, when he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached;
when he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached;
when he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached.
“Monks, this is called a learned noble disciple who is detached from birth, aging, and death; detached from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; detached from suffering, I say.
This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intention, this is the difference between a learned noble disciple and an unlearned worldling.
The wise one does not experience [craving] feeling.”
Happiness as well as suffering, and even great learning—
this is the great distinction between the wise person skilled in means and the worldling.
For one who has mastered the Dhamma, who is learned,
and who clearly sees this world and the next,
desirable things do not disturb the mind.
What is unlovely does not provoke resistance in him.
Through his lack of attachment or aversion, [those states] are utterly consumed,
have come to an end, and no longer exist.
Having known the stainless and sorrowless state,
one who has gone beyond existence understands it rightly.
Thus ends the sixth [verse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 36.7 (SN 36.7, PTS SN iv 210) 1. Sagāthāvagga Paṭhamagelaññasutta (The First Discourse on Illness) At Sāvatthī. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was staying near Sāvatthī at Jīvakambavana, the park of Jīvaka Komārabhacca. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: “Moggallāna, is your body free from illness? Is it comfortable? Do you have strength? Does your bodily vigor not diminish? Are you able to endure it? Are you able to carry on? “Bhante, my body is not free from illness; it is painful. My bodily vigor has diminished, and I am unable to endure it or carry on. “Moggallāna, what is the cause, what is the reason, why your bodily vigor has diminished and you are unable to endure it or carry on? “Bhante, for a long time I have been afflicted by a chronic illness. Because of that, my bodily vigor has diminished and I am unable to endure it or carry on. “Moggallāna, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is capable of attaining the destruction of the taints in this very life. What four? Here, Moggallāna, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. “When a noble disciple possesses these four things, Moggallāna, he is capable of attaining the destruction of the taints in this very life. “Bhante, I possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... I possess the virtues dear to the noble ones. But, Bhante, I do not see any other ascetic or brahmin who possesses such confirmed confidence in the Buddha as I do, nor such confirmed confidence in the Dhamma... nor such confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha... nor such virtues dear to the noble ones as I do. Yet, Bhante, I am not one who has attained the destruction of the taints. “Moggallāna, it is not easy to understand the mind of another, the nature of another, the disposition of another. It is difficult to know: ‘This person will attain the destruction of the taints in this very life. “Bhante, I have heard this from the Blessed One’s own lips: ‘It is not easy to understand the mind of another, the nature of another, the disposition of another. It is difficult to know: “This person will attain the destruction of the taints in this very life. “Moggallāna, I have taught you the Dhamma in its various aspects, analyzed it, made it plain, revealed it, and explained it. You should train yourself in it in such a way that, with the destruction of the taints, you might realize for yourselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwell therein. “Bhante, I have heard this from the Blessed One’s own lips: ‘It is not easy to understand the mind of another, the nature of another, the disposition of another. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Gabled Hall.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the sick ward; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should await his time mindful and clearly comprehending.
This is our instruction to you.
And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful?”
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … pe … he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind … pe …
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
In this way, monks, a monk is mindful.
And how, monks, is a monk clearly comprehending?
Here, monks, a monk acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating.
He acts with clear comprehension; whether walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, he acts with clear comprehension.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk acts with clear comprehension.
A monk, monks, mindful and clearly comprehending, should await his time.
This is our instruction to you.
Now, monks, if while that bhikkhu dwells thus mindful, clearly comprehending, diligent, ardent, and resolute, a pleasant feeling arises, he understands:
‘This pleasant feeling has arisen in me.’
And that indeed arises dependently, not independently.
Dependent on what?
Dependent on this very body.
‘Moreover, this body is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
How could a pleasant feeling that has arisen dependent on this body—which is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen—be permanent?
Thus he dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in pleasant feeling; he dwells contemplating vanishing, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 36.17 (SN 36.17, PTS SN iv 221) 2. Rahogatavagga First Discourse on Being Much Together “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging, I say that those ascetics or brahmins are not enlightened. And why is that? Because, bhikkhus, it is by understanding as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging that one is called an enlightened one. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging. It is in this way that you should train yourselves.”

Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“What, venerable sir, is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the way leading to the cessation of feeling?
What is the gratification in feeling? What is the danger in feeling? What is the escape from feeling?”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
These, bhikkhus, are called feelings.”
With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling;
with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of feeling, namely: [the rest of the eight factors].
Right view … [and so on] … right concentration.

That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in feeling.

Furthermore, monks, the gradual cessation of formations has been declared by me:

for one who has attained the first jhāna, speech is tranquilized.
For one who has attained the second jhāna, applied thought and sustained thought have subsided.
For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture has subsided.
For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, inhalation and exhalation have subsided.
“For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have subsided.
For a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, lust has subsided, hatred has subsided, and delusion has subsided. Thus it was said.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 36.19 (SN 36.19, PTS SN iv 223) 2.
Rahogatavagga (The Chapter on Solitude)
The Discourse to Pañcakaṅga.
Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga approached the Venerable Udāyī;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Udāyī and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
“How many kinds of feeling, venerable Udāyin, have been spoken of by the Blessed One?
“Three kinds of feeling, master carpenter, have been spoken of by the Blessed One:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”
“These, carpenter, are the three feelings spoken of by the Blessed One.
When this was said, the carpenter Pañcakanga said to the Venerable Udāyin:
“Venerable Udāyin, it is not the case that three feelings were spoken of by the Blessed One.”
“Two kinds of feeling have been spoken of by the Blessed One—
the pleasant feeling and the painful feeling.
As for this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, it has been spoken of by the Blessed One as peaceful and sublime pleasure.”
A second time, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the carpenter Pañcakanga:
"Carpenter, two feelings were not taught by the Blessed One.
Three feelings were taught by the Blessed One."
“Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
these three feelings were spoken of by the Blessed One.
A second time, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga said this to the Venerable Udāyin:
“Venerable Udāyin, it was not three feelings that were spoken of by the Blessed One.
Two feelings were spoken of by the Blessed One—
the pleasant feeling and the painful feeling.”
“Venerable sir, this feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant has been called by the Blessed One a peaceful and sublime pleasure.
For a third time, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the carpenter Pañcakanga:
“Carpenter, two kinds of feeling have not been taught by the Blessed One.”
“Three feelings have been spoken of by the Blessed One:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
these three feelings have been spoken of by the Blessed One.”
A third time, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga said this to the Venerable Udāyin:
"Venerable Udāyin, three feelings were not taught by the Blessed One.
Two feelings were taught by the Blessed One: [pleasant feeling and painful feeling]."
“There is pleasant feeling and painful feeling.
But as for this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, it has been called by the Blessed One a peaceful and sublime pleasure.
Neither was the Venerable Udāyī able to convince the carpenter Pañcakanga, nor was the carpenter Pañcakanga able to convince the Venerable Udāyī.
The Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between the Venerable Udāyī and Pañcakanga the carpenter.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between the Venerable Udāyī and Pañcakanga the carpenter.
“Ānanda, it was indeed a correct explanation that the carpenter Pañcakaṅga did not approve of the bhikkhu Udāyī’s [statement],
and it was also a correct explanation that the bhikkhu Udāyī did not approve of the carpenter Pañcakaṅga’s [statement]. For,
Ānanda, I have spoken of two kinds of feeling by way of a method.”
In one way, three feelings have been taught by me;
in another way, five feelings have been taught by me;
in yet another way, six feelings have been taught by me.
Eighteen kinds of feeling have been taught by me by way of exposition.
Thirty-six kinds of feeling have been taught by me by way of exposition.
One hundred and eight kinds of feeling have been taught by me by way of exposition.
"Thus, Ānanda, has the Dhamma been taught by me through various methods. Since the Dhamma has been taught by me through various methods,
it is to be expected that those who do not approve of, do not acknowledge, and do not rejoice in what has been well-spoken and well-uttered by one another will fall into quarrels."
"Having fallen into quarrels and disputes, they will dwell piercing one another with the weapons of the tongue.
Thus, Ānanda, has the Dhamma been taught by me through various methods.
And since the Dhamma has been taught by me through such various methods, those who [speak] what is well-spoken and well-uttered to one another...
They will approve of it, they will consent to it, and they will rejoice in it; for this is to be expected of them:
that they will dwell together in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed, looking upon one another with eyes of love.
Ānanda, these are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; ...
[and so on] ... tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
"These, Ānanda, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent upon these five cords of sensual pleasure—
this is called sensual pleasure."
Ānanda, as for those who would say,
"They experience this as the highest possible peaceful happiness and joy," I do not concede that to them.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness?

"Here, Ānanda, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
This, Ānanda, is a happiness more excellent and sublime than that other happiness.
And those, Ānanda, who might say: [this is the highest happiness]," [would be speaking incorrectly].
‘They experience this as the highest possible peace, happiness, and joy’—
this I do not concede to them. And why is that?
“There is, Ānanda, another happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness?

Here, Ānanda, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.”
This, Ānanda, is a happiness more excellent and sublime than that previous happiness.
As for those, Ānanda, who might say:
‘They experience this as the highest possible peace, happiness, and joy’—
I do not approve of this for them. Why is that?
Ānanda, there is another happiness, more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness?
Here, Ānanda, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending;

he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness. This is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than the former.
He enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
This, Ānanda, is a happiness more excellent and sublime than that other happiness.
Now, Ānanda, those who might say:
‘They experience this as the highest possible peace, happiness, and joy’—
this I do not grant them. And why is that?
“There is, Ānanda, another happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness?

Here, Ānanda, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.”
"Ānanda, this other happiness is indeed more excellent and more sublime than that happiness.
Ānanda, as for those who would say:
'They experience this as the highest possible peaceful happiness and joy'—"
I do not approve of this for them. Why is that?
Ānanda, there is another happiness, more excellent and more sublime than this one.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness which is more excellent and sublime than this happiness?

Here, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This, Ānanda, is that other happiness which is more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
Ānanda, as for those who might say,
‘They experience this as the highest possible peace, happiness,
and joy,’ I do not grant them that.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness?
In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking, "consciousness is infinite," enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
This, Ānanda, is a happiness more excellent and sublime than that other happiness.
Now, Ānanda, those who might say:
‘They experience this as the highest possible peace, happiness, and joy’—
this I do not concede to them. And why is that?
“There is, Ānanda, another happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving ‘there is nothing,’ enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.”
"Ānanda, this other happiness is indeed more excellent and more sublime than that happiness.
Ānanda, as for those who would say:
'They experience only this much as the highest peaceful happiness and joy'—"
This I do not authorize for them. And why is that?
Ānanda, there is another happiness, more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness which is more excellent and sublime than this happiness?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This, Ānanda, is that other happiness which is more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
“Ānanda, as for those who would say,
‘They experience this as the highest possible peaceful happiness and joy,’ I do not grant them this.”
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness?
"Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
This, Ānanda, is a happiness more excellent and sublime than that other happiness.
Now it is possible, Ānanda, that wanderers of other sects might say this:"
“The ascetic Gotama speaks of the cessation of perception and feeling, and he describes that as happiness.
What is this? How is this? Ānanda, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be addressed as follows:
“Friend, it is not with reference to pleasant feeling alone that the Blessed One describes pleasure.
Rather, friend, wherever and in whatever way pleasure is found, the Tathāgata describes that as pleasure.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 36.20 (SN 36.20, PTS SN iv 228) 2. Rahogatavagga Bhikkhusutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is dwelling in solitude, he should reflect thus: ‘I am now dwelling alone; let me not give rise to any evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is mindful and clearly comprehending in regard to his own self. “Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is dwelling in solitude, he should reflect thus: ‘I am now dwelling alone; let me not give rise to any evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen. “Bhikkhus, by way of exposition, I have spoken of two feelings; by way of exposition, I have spoken of three feelings;

3. The Chapter on the Method of One Hundred and Eight:
The Discourse to Sīvaka.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, there are certain recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:”
“Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
What does Master Gotama say about this?
“Sīvaka, here too some feelings arise originating from bile.”
This, Sīvaka, should also be understood: that here certain feelings arise originating from bile.
This, Sīvaka, is also recognized as true by the world: that here certain feelings arise originating from bile.
In this regard, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: [as follows]...
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
They overstep both what they have known for themselves and what is considered true in the world.
Therefore, I say that the views of those recluses and brahmins are wrong.
“Furthermore, Sīvaka, there are [diseases] originating from bile...
Furthermore, Sīvaka, there are [diseases] originating from wind...
Furthermore, Sīvaka, there are [diseases] arising from a combination [of the humors]...”
“Sīvaka, there are indeed [diseases] born of a change in the seasons...
Sīvaka, there are indeed [diseases] born of the improper handling of food...
Sīvaka, there are indeed [diseases] resulting from external trauma...”
“Sīvaka, here certain feelings born of the ripening of kamma also arise.
This, Sīvaka, should be understood by oneself:
that here certain feelings born of the ripening of kamma also arise.”
This, Sīvaka, is also considered true by the world:
that here some feelings arise born of the ripening of kamma.
In this regard, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view [speak as follows]:
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
They overreach both what they have known for themselves and what is considered true in the world.
Therefore, I say that those ascetics and brahmins are wrong.”
When this was said, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
“Bile, phlegm, and wind,
the humors combined, and the seasons;
irregularity, and that caused by external assault.”

3. The Chapter on the Exposition of One Hundred and Eight. The Discourse on One Hundred and Eight:
“Monks, I shall teach you the exposition of the Dhamma consisting of one hundred and eight points.”
Listen to that.
And what, bhikkhus, is the discourse on the Dharma consisting of one hundred and eight points?
Bhikkhus, by way of a method, I have spoken of two kinds of feeling as well.
In one way, three kinds of feeling have been taught by me;
in another way, five kinds of feeling have been taught by me;
in yet another way, six kinds of feeling have been taught by me.
I have spoken of eighteen feelings by way of a method;
I have spoken of thirty-six feelings by way of a method;
I have spoken of one hundred and eight feelings by way of a method.
And what, monks, are the two kinds of feeling?
Bodily and mental— these, monks,
are called the two kinds of feeling.
And what, monks, are the three feelings?
Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
these, monks, are called the three feelings.
And what, monks, are the five feelings?
The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief, and the faculty of equanimity—
these, monks, are called the five feelings.
And what, monks, are the six feelings?
Feeling born of eye-contact …pe… feeling born of mind-contact.
These, monks, are called the six feelings.
And what, monks, are the eighteen feelings?
Six explorations of joy, six explorations of grief, and six explorations of equanimity.
These, monks, are called the eighteen feelings.
And what, monks, are the thirty-six feelings?

Six kinds of joy based on the household life, six kinds of joy based on renunciation; six kinds of grief based on the household life, six kinds of grief based on renunciation; six kinds of equanimity based on the household life, and six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation.
These, monks, are called the thirty-six feelings.
And what, monks, is the hundred and eight feelings?
The thirty-six past feelings, the thirty-six future feelings, and the thirty-six present feelings.
“Monks, these are called the one hundred and eight feelings.
This, monks, is the discourse on the Dharma consisting of the exposition of the one hundred and eight.
The second [sutta].

This too is called ‘mindfulness of the body. “Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, this occurred to me:

‘What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of feeling?
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘There are these three kinds of feeling:’

Saṁyutta Nikāya 36.25 (SN 36.25, SN 36.24b, PTS SN iv 233) 3. Aṭṭhasatapariyāyavagga Ñāṇasutta (The Discourse on Knowledge) “Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What four? Edible food, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. “Bhikkhus, when one knows and sees these four nutriments as they really are, and knows and sees the origin of these four nutriments as it really is, and knows and sees the cessation of these four nutriments as it really is, and knows and sees the way leading to the cessation of these four nutriments as it really is—then, bhikkhus, that noble disciple is called one who possesses knowledge, one who sees, one who has arrived at this Dhamma, one who dwells in this Dhamma, a noble hearer who has attained the path.”
“‘These are feelings,’ monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
‘This is the origin of feelings,’ monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye … light.
‘This is the way leading to the origin of feelings,’ monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye … light.”
“‘This is the cessation of feeling,’ monks—regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in me ...
‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling,’ monks—regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in me ...
‘This is the gratification in feeling,’ monks—regarding these things unheard of before ...”
“‘This is the danger in feeling,’ monks—regarding these things unheard of before...
‘This indeed is the escape’—regarding these things unheard of before, monks, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
The fifth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 36.26 (SN 36.26, SN 36.25, PTS SN iv 234) 3. Aṭṭhasatapariyāyavagga Sambahulabhikkhusutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is capable of abandoning the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to views; he is capable of entering and dwelling in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. What five? Here, a bhikkhu has faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults. Having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and provisions for the sick. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. These are the five qualities with which a bhikkhu is endowed that enable him to abandon the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to views; that enables him to enter and dwell in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints.”
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached, ... [as before] ... seated to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:

What is the way leading to the cessation of feeling?"
“What is the gratification in feeling, what is the danger, and what is the escape?
“Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

With the arising of contact there is the arising of feeling.
Craving is the way leading to the arising of feeling.
"With the cessation of contact...
[as before] ...the removal of desire and lust for feeling, the abandoning of desire and lust for feeling—this is the escape from feeling.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 36.27 (SN 36.27, SN 36.26, PTS SN iv 234) 3. The Chapter on the Exposition of One Hundred and Eight The First Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins “Monks, there are these four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world. What four? “There is the case where a certain ascetic or brahmin, having abandoned the lower seven fetters, is of such a nature that he will attain final knowledge (*parinibbāna*) right here in this very life. This is the first kind of ascetic and brahmin to be found existing in the world. “Then again, there is the case where a certain ascetic or brahmin, having abandoned the lower seven fetters, is of such a nature that—with the total destruction of the five lower fetters—he will reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and, attaining finality there, will not return from that world. This is the second kind of ascetic and brahmin to be found existing in the world. “Then again, there is the case where a certain ascetic or brahmin, having abandoned the lower seven fetters, is of such a nature that—with the total destruction of three fetters and with the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion—he will become a once-returner, who, after returning to this world only one more time, will put an end to suffering. This is the third kind of ascetic and brahmin to be found existing in the world. “Then again, there is the case where a certain ascetic or brahmin, having abandoned the lower seven fetters, is of such a nature that—with the total destruction of three fetters—he will become a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for awakening, assured, headed for full enlightenment. This is the fourth kind of ascetic and brahmin to be found existing in the world. “These, monks, are the four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings.
Which three?
Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”
"Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand, as they really are, the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these three feelings— they, monks,
are neither ascetics among ascetics nor brahmins among brahmins,
nor do those venerable ones, in this very life, attain the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood."
They dwell having personally realized and attained these phenomena through direct knowledge.

And as for those recluses or brahmins, monks, who understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these three feelings— they, monks,
among recluses are truly accounted as recluses, and among brahmins as brahmins.

And they are esteemed as brahmins. Furthermore, those venerable ones, having realized for themselves through direct higher knowledge in this very life the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood, dwell having attained them.
Thus ends the seventh [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 36.28 (SN 36.28, SN 36.27, PTS SN iv 235) 3. Aṭṭhasatapariyāyavagga Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world. What four? The one who is a mere renunciant by way of livelihood; the one who is a mere renunciant by way of outward appearance; the one who is a mere renunciant by way of verbal expression; and the one who is a true renunciant. And how, bhikkhus, is one a mere renunciant by way of livelihood? Here, someone goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, but he does not train himself in accordance with the Dhamma, does not live in accordance with the Dhamma, does not master the higher virtuous behavior, the higher concentration, and the higher wisdom. He does not experience with his own direct knowledge the unexcelled liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life for which, having gone forth, he trains himself. This is called a mere renunciant by way of livelihood. And how, bhikkhus, is one a mere renunciant by way of outward appearance? Here, someone goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, and he trains himself in accordance with the Dhamma, lives in accordance with the Dhamma, and masters the higher virtuous behavior, the higher concentration, and the higher wisdom; yet he does not experience with his own direct knowledge the unexcelled liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life for which, having gone forth, he trains himself. This is called a mere renunciant by way of outward appearance. And how, bhikkhus, is one a mere renunciant by way of verbal expression? Here, someone goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, and he trains himself in accordance with the Dhamma, lives in accordance with the Dhamma, and masters the higher virtuous behavior, the higher concentration, and the higher wisdom; and he experiences with his own direct knowledge the unexcelled liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life for which, having gone forth, he trains himself; yet he does not declare this to others, does not proclaim it, does not reveal it, does not establish it, does not disclose it, does not analyze it, and does not explain it in detail. This is called a mere renunciant by way of verbal expression. And how, bhikkhus, is one a true renunciant? Here, someone goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, and he trains himself in accordance with the Dhamma, lives in accordance with the Dhamma, and masters the higher virtuous behavior, the higher concentration, and the higher wisdom; and he experiences with his own direct knowledge the unexcelled liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life for which, having gone forth, he trains himself; and he declares this to others, proclaims it, reveals it, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, and explains it in detail. This is called a true renunciant. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings.
Which three?
Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”
“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these three feelings...
[they do not realize the goal]. But those who understand them... having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, enter and dwell in that state.
The eighth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 36.29 (SN 36.29, SN 36.28, PTS SN iv 235) 3. The Chapter on the Exposition of One Hundred and Eight The Third Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world. What four? The one who is a mere renunciant by way of livelihood; the one who is a renunciant through faith; the one who is a renunciant through the search for a doctrine; and the one who is a renunciant through the realization of the Dhamma. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ascetic and brahmin who is a mere renunciant by way of livelihood? Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, having shaved off his hair and beard, having put on the saffron robes, goes forth from the home life into homelessness. He lives supported by the gains of others, dependent on others for his livelihood. This is called, bhikkhus, an ascetic and brahmin who is a mere renunciant by way of livelihood. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ascetic and brahmin who is a renunciant through faith? Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, having shaved off his hair and beard, having put on the saffron robes, goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘I am one who has gone forth. This is called, bhikkhus, an ascetic and brahmin who is a renunciant through faith. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ascetic and brahmin who is a renunciant through the search for a doctrine? Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, having shaved off his hair and beard, having put on the saffron robes, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, seeking a teacher, seeking a doctrine, thinking: ‘I shall learn the Dhamma. This is called, bhikkhus, an ascetic and brahmin who is a renunciant through the search for a doctrine. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ascetic and brahmin who is a renunciant through the realization of the Dhamma? Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, having shaved off his hair and beard, having put on the saffron robes, goes forth from the home life into homelessness. Having gone forth, he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults. Having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He dwells with his sense faculties guarded, with mindfulness established, possessing a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing. He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Having understood as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ having understood as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ having understood as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ having understood as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. This is called, bhikkhus, an ascetic and brahmin who is a renunciant through the realization of the Dhamma. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins do not understand feeling, do not understand the origin of feeling, do not understand the cessation of feeling,

and do not understand the way leading to the cessation of feeling … [as before] … [but those who] understand … [and so on] … having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, enter upon and abide in that state. Thus was the ninth [sutta].
Saṃyutta Nikāya 36.30 (SN 36.30, SN 36.29a, PTS SN iv 235) 3. Aṭṭhasatapariyāyavagga Suddhikasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these six elements. What six?
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element. These, bhikkhus, are the six elements.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings.
Which three?
Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”
“Monks, these indeed are the three feelings.
The Tenth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 36.31 (SN 36.31, SN 36.29b, PTS SN iv 235)
3. The Chapter on the Method of One Hundred and Eight: The Discourse on the Non-Material.
“Monks, there is material rapture, there is non-material rapture, and there is non-material rapture that is even more non-material.”
There is worldly happiness, there is unworldly happiness, and there is unworldly happiness that is more unworldly than the other;
there is worldly equanimity, there is unworldly equanimity, and there is unworldly equanimity that is more unworldly than the other;
there is worldly liberation, there is unworldly liberation, and there is unworldly liberation that is more unworldly than the other.
And what, monks, is sensual rapture?
There are these five cords of sensual pleasure, monks.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; ...
[and so on] ... tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
“Monks, whatever rapture arises dependent upon these five cords of sensual pleasure, this, monks, is called carnal rapture.
And what, monks, is spiritual rapture?

Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.”

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied thought and without sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
This, monks, is called rapture that is not worldly.
And what, monks, is rapture that is even more unworldly than the unworldly?
“Monks, when a monk whose taints are destroyed reviews his mind as liberated from lust, reviews his mind as liberated from hatred,
and reviews his mind as liberated from delusion, the rapture that arises— this, monks,
is called rapture that is unworldly and more unworldly than the unworldly.”
And what, monks, is sensual pleasure?
There are these five strands of sensual pleasure, monks.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust...
[and so on] ...tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
“Monks, whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent upon these five cords of sensual pleasure, this, monks, is called carnal happiness.
And what, monks, is spiritual happiness?

Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.”

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness"; thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
This, monks, is called spiritual happiness.
And what, monks, is spiritual happiness that is even more spiritual than the former?
It is, monks, when a monk whose taints are destroyed reviews his mind as liberated from lust and liberated from hatred... [and so forth].
For one who reviews the liberated mind, for one who reviews the mind liberated from delusion, pleasure and joy arise.
This, monks, is called spiritual happiness that is more spiritual than the non-spiritual.
And what, monks, is spiritual equanimity?
“Monks, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust... [and so on for the other sense objects]...”
Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Whatever equanimity arises dependent upon these five strands of sensual pleasure, this, monks, is called worldly equanimity.
And what, monks, is spiritual equanimity?
Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This, monks, is called equanimity that is unworldly.
And what, monks, is equanimity that is even more unworldly than the unworldly?
It is, monks, when a monk whose taints are destroyed reviews his mind as liberated from lust and from hatred.
When one reviews the mind as liberated, or reviews the mind as liberated from delusion, equanimity arises;
this, monks, is called equanimity that is more unworldly than the unworldly.
And what, monks, is the worldly liberation?
The liberation associated with form is the carnal liberation.
And what, bhikkhus, is the non-carnal liberation?
The liberation associated with the formless is the non-carnal liberation.
And what, monks, is the liberation that is more unworldly than the unworldly?
It is the liberation that arises, monks, when a monk whose taints are destroyed reviews his mind as liberated from lust,
reviews his mind as liberated from hatred, and reviews his mind as liberated from delusion.
“This, monks, is called the unworldly liberation that is even more unworldly.
The eleventh [sutta].

and formerly the knowledge by the monk.
